---
title: "Simulating an Orchestrated Platform"
---

Long waits and physical measurements are two reasons laboratory code is difficult to test quickly.
This chapter substitutes simulated time and stochastic measurements, then combines them with the
run directory of [chapter 13](13_record_runs.qmd), the SQLite tables of
[chapter 14](14_state_in_sqlite.qmd), and the wrappers of
[chapter 15](15_compose_behaviour.qmd) into a single simulated unit operation: a normalization cell
fed by a plate stacker.

## Setup {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: cell-setup
#| output: false
import json, logging, random, sqlite3, tempfile
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from pylabrobot.liquid_handling import LiquidHandler
from pylabrobot.liquid_handling.backends import LiquidHandlerChatterboxBackend
from pylabrobot.resources import (
    STARLetDeck, PLT_CAR_L5AC_A00, cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb,
    nest_1_troughplate_195000uL_Vb, TIP_CAR_288_C00,
    opentrons_96_filtertiprack_200ul, ResourceStack, Coordinate,
    set_volume_tracking, set_tip_tracking,
)

scratch = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="cookbook_platform_"))
print("scratch:", scratch)
```

---

## Simulate time and data together {#simulation}

::: {.recipe}

A minimal simulated clock:

```{python}
#| label: cell-simclock
class SimClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.time = 0.0

    def now(self):
        return self.time

    def advance(self, seconds):
        self.time += seconds

    def advance_to(self, when):
        self.time = max(self.time, when)
```

Instead of asking the operating system what time it is — `now = clock.now()` — and instead of
actually waiting five minutes — `clock.advance(300)` — the protocol depends on the clock object, so
either version can be substituted.

The same idea applies to measurements. Every quantification carries error, so a simulated reading is
a true value plus noise:

```{python}
#| label: cell-simread
rng = random.Random(42)          # <1>

def quantify(true_conc, cv=0.03):
    return true_conc * (
        1 + rng.gauss(0, cv)
    )
```

1. Seeding the random-number generator gives the simulation stochastic behaviour while keeping a
   failing test reproducible.

For example, quantifying the same sample four times:

```{python}
#| label: cell-simread-run
for _ in range(4):
    print(round(quantify(48.0), 2))
```

Re-seeding reproduces the identical sequence, which is what makes an assertion about simulated data
worth writing at all:

```{python}
#| label: cell-simread-repeat
rng = random.Random(42)
print([round(quantify(48.0), 2) for _ in range(4)])
```

**See also:** `pylabrobot.io.capture` in [chapter 12](../part2/12_hardware.qmd) records real device
I/O for replay, which is the hardware-level counterpart to this.

:::

---

## Simulate a normalization cell {#platform}

::: {.recipe}

The pieces can now be combined into one unit operation of the kind that sits in a real pipeline.

Plates of extracted DNA arrive from upstream at times nobody controls. Each well has a known
concentration, measured before the plate got here and supplied with it. The cell dilutes every well
to a target concentration with buffer, then sets the plate down on the output side.

```text
arrivals ──► input stacker ──► liquid handler ──► output stacker
             (plate hotel)      (dilute to target)
```

Three pieces of the platform are in that diagram, and only one of them pipettes. The arrival stream
stands in for whatever runs upstream — an extraction cell, a quantification step, an operator with a
trolley — reduced to the two things this cell needs from it: when a plate shows up, and what is in
it. The stackers are the interface to the rest of the platform on either side, and as the last
section shows, the input stacker decides more about how this cell behaves than any of the code does.

What none of it needs is a scheduler. The decisions here are per-well arithmetic, and the plate that
runs next is whichever one the gripper can reach. What the cell does need is somewhere to record
what happened, and a way to run several hours of arrivals in a fraction of a second.

### Build the cell

The STAR's iSWAP moves the plates, so transport and pipetting contend for one instrument: the arm
cannot fetch the next plate while the head is dispensing. Everything else in the cell — carrier,
trough, tips, both stackers — is passive labware with no backend behind it.

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-deck
#| output: false
lh = LiquidHandler(
    backend=LiquidHandlerChatterboxBackend(),
    deck=STARLetDeck(),
)
await lh.setup()

carrier = PLT_CAR_L5AC_A00(name="carrier")
lh.deck.assign_child_resource(carrier, rails=10)
carrier[0] = buffer = nest_1_troughplate_195000uL_Vb(
    name="buffer"
)

tip_carrier = TIP_CAR_288_C00(name="tip_carrier")
lh.deck.assign_child_resource(tip_carrier, rails=2)
tip_carrier[0] = rack = opentrons_96_filtertiprack_200ul(
    name="rack"
)
```

The two stackers are `ResourceStack`s, and PLR is explicit about what that means — from its own
docstring:

> Stacks growing in the z direction are from bottom to top, and function as the
> [stack data type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(abstract_data_type)).

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-stackers
#| output: false
inp = ResourceStack(name="input_stacker", direction="z")
out = ResourceStack(name="output_stacker", direction="z")

lh.deck.assign_child_resource(
    inp, location=Coordinate(600, 300, 100)
)
lh.deck.assign_child_resource(
    out, location=Coordinate(600, 100, 100)
)

set_volume_tracking(True)
set_tip_tracking(True)
buffer["A1"][0].set_volume(195_000)
```

A stacker is not a machine. There is no backend and no `setup()` — the same idea as the magnet in
[chapter 9](../part2/09_moving_labware.qmd#magnet), where state is expressed by position rather than
by command. What makes it a stack is that gravity leaves exactly one plate reachable, and PLR
enforces that rather than trusting the protocol:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-stack-guard
#| error: true
probe = cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb(name="probe")
inp.assign_child_resource(probe)
inp.assign_child_resource(
    cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb(name="probe_2")
)

inp.unassign_child_resource(probe)     # not the top item
```

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-stack-clear
#| output: false
for child in list(reversed(inp.children)):
    inp.unassign_child_resource(child)
```

### The dilution is arithmetic

Each well holds `V_SAMPLE` µL at a known concentration. Diluting to `TARGET` means adding buffer
until the volume has grown by the ratio of the two concentrations. It is worth keeping this as a
plain function of numbers — no robot, no database, no clock — because it is the part that can be
wrong:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-plan
TARGET, V_SAMPLE, WELL_MAX = 10.0, 10.0, 360.0

def plan_well(conc):
    if conc <= TARGET:                                  # <1>
        return 0.0, "under"

    buffer_vol = V_SAMPLE * (conc / TARGET - 1)

    if V_SAMPLE + buffer_vol > WELL_MAX:                # <2>
        return 0.0, "overflow"

    return round(buffer_vol, 1), "ok"                   # <3>
```

1. A well already at or below target cannot be brought *up* by dilution. It goes forward untouched
   and flagged, because the honest output of a normalization step is "here is what I could not do".
2. The other bound is the labware. A sample concentrated enough to need more buffer than the well
   holds needs an intermediate transfer, which this cell does not do.
3. Channels dispense in 0.1 µL steps, so the plan is rounded to what the instrument can actually
   deliver.

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-plan-run
for conc in [48.0, 112.4, 9.1, 6000.0]:
    print(conc, plan_well(conc))
```

### Record the run

The run directory and the process log are [chapter 13](13_record_runs.qmd); the tables are
[chapter 14](14_state_in_sqlite.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-run-dir
#| output: false
run_id = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
run_dir = scratch / "runs" / run_id
(run_dir / "logs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

log = logging.getLogger(f"run.{run_id}")
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
log.propagate = False
log.addHandler(
    logging.FileHandler(run_dir / "logs" / "process.log")
)

db = sqlite3.connect(run_dir / "run.sqlite")

db.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE plates (
        plate     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        arrived   REAL,
        concs     TEXT,
        loaded    INTEGER,
        started   REAL,
        finished  REAL
    )
""")

db.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE wells (
        plate     TEXT,
        well      INTEGER,
        conc      REAL,
        buffer    REAL,
        flag      TEXT,
        achieved  REAL
    )
""")
```

Arrivals are a seeded stream of times and concentrations — the upstream process, reduced to the only
two things this cell needs from it:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-arrivals
sim_rng = random.Random(42)
MEAN_GAP, SERVICE = 120, 300           # <1>

t = 0.0
for i in range(6):
    t += sim_rng.expovariate(1 / MEAN_GAP)
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO plates(plate, arrived, concs) VALUES (?,?,?)",
        (
            f"plate_{i+1}",
            t,
            json.dumps([
                max(1.0, sim_rng.gauss(60, 25))
                for _ in range(8)
            ]),
        ),
    )
db.commit()

for row in db.execute("SELECT plate, arrived FROM plates ORDER BY arrived"):
    print(row[0], round(row[1]))
```

1. Plates arrive faster than the cell can process them. That is the interesting case — with a gap
   longer than the service time the stacker never holds more than one plate and nothing below is
   visible.

### Load and process

Upstream sets each arrived plate on top of the input stacker. The robot is not involved:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-load
def load_arrivals(now):
    rows = db.execute(
        """
        SELECT plate, concs FROM plates
        WHERE arrived <= ? AND loaded IS NULL
        ORDER BY arrived
        """,
        (now,),
    ).fetchall()

    for plate_id, concs in rows:
        plate = cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb(name=plate_id)

        for i in range(8):
            plate[i][0].set_volume(V_SAMPLE)

        inp.assign_child_resource(plate)
        db.execute(
            "UPDATE plates SET loaded=1 WHERE plate=?",
            (plate_id,),
        )
    db.commit()
```

One plate through the cell. `handle_errors` is the wrapper from
[chapter 15](15_compose_behaviour.qmd#recovery); the wells that need no buffer are dropped from
`use_channels` rather than dispensed with a token volume:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-normalize
#| output: false
import functools

def handle_errors(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return await fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except Exception:
            log.exception("%s failed", fn.__name__)
            raise
    return wrapper

@handle_errors
async def normalize(plate, concs, spots):
    rows = [plan_well(c) for c in concs]
    need = [i for i, (vol, _) in enumerate(rows) if vol > 0]     # <1>
    vols = [rows[i][0] for i in need]

    await lh.pick_up_tips(
        [spots[i] for i in need], use_channels=need
    )
    await lh.aspirate(
        [buffer["A1"][0]] * len(need),
        vols=vols,
        use_channels=need,
    )
    await lh.dispense(
        [plate[i][0] for i in need],
        vols=vols,
        use_channels=need,
    )
    await lh.discard_tips(use_channels=need)

    return rows
```

1. `use_channels` must match the length of `vols`; a well that needs nothing is simply not a channel
   in this operation.

### Run it

The loop has no scheduler in it. When the stacker is empty the clock jumps to the next arrival;
otherwise the top plate is taken. **The hardware chooses which plate runs**, and the loop only
records the consequence:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-run
#| output: false
clock = SimClock()
column = 1

while True:
    load_arrivals(clock.now())

    if len(inp.children) == 0:
        nxt = db.execute(
            "SELECT MIN(arrived) FROM plates WHERE finished IS NULL"
        ).fetchone()[0]

        if nxt is None:
            break

        clock.advance_to(nxt)                                    # <1>
        continue

    plate = inp.get_top_item()                                   # <2>
    arrived, concs = db.execute(
        "SELECT arrived, concs FROM plates WHERE plate=?",
        (plate.name,),
    ).fetchone()

    started = clock.now()
    await lh.move_plate(plate, carrier[1])

    rows = await normalize(
        plate, json.loads(concs), rack[f"A{column}:H{column}"]
    )
    column += 1

    await lh.move_plate(plate, out)
    clock.advance(SERVICE)

    for i, ((vol, flag), conc) in enumerate(zip(rows, json.loads(concs))):
        db.execute(
            "INSERT INTO wells VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (
                plate.name, i, conc, vol, flag,
                quantify(conc * V_SAMPLE / (V_SAMPLE + vol)),    # <3>
            ),
        )

    db.execute(
        "UPDATE plates SET started=?, finished=? WHERE plate=?",
        (started, clock.now(), plate.name),
    )
    db.commit()
    log.info(
        "%s waited %.0f s", plate.name, started - arrived
    )
```

1. No sleeping. Idle time is a jump.
2. `get_top_item()` is the only plate the gripper can reach.
3. The achieved concentration is what the dilution actually produced, seen through a quantification
   with the noise from the first recipe.

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-results
for plate_id, arrived, started in db.execute(
    "SELECT plate, arrived, started FROM plates ORDER BY arrived"
):
    print(
        f"{plate_id}  arrived {arrived:6.0f}  "
        f"started {started:6.0f}  waited {started - arrived:6.0f}"
    )
```

### Test process invariants

The exact numbers depend on the seeded arrivals; these properties do not.

Every plate was processed, and none before it arrived:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-invariant-order
assert db.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plates WHERE finished IS NULL"
).fetchone()[0] == 0

assert db.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plates WHERE started < arrived"
).fetchone()[0] == 0
print("every plate processed, none before it arrived")
```

Every well reached target or was flagged:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-invariant-target
for conc, vol, flag, achieved in db.execute(
    "SELECT conc, buffer, flag, achieved FROM wells"
):
    if flag == "ok":
        assert abs(achieved - TARGET) / TARGET <= 0.10           # <1>
print("every unflagged well within 10% of target")
```

1. The tolerance has to cover the 0.1 µL rounding in `plan_well` *and* the quantification noise. A
   tolerance tighter than the measurement is a test that fails for no reason.

Nothing teleported — the plates are physically where the protocol believes:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-invariant-position
assert len(inp.children) == 0
assert len(out.children) == 6
assert carrier[1].resource is None
print("input stacker drained, six plates on the output stacker, deck clear")
```

That last one is worth more than it looks. Chatterbox validates *state*, not physics
([chapter 1](../part1/01_robot_on_screen.qmd#workcell)) — it will happily print a move that could
never happen. The resource tree is what catches it.

### A stacker is a stack

The plates did not come out in the order they went in:

```{python}
#| label: cell-cell-fifo
order = db.execute(
    "SELECT arrived, started FROM plates ORDER BY started"
).fetchall()

fifo = all(a <= b for (a, _), (b, _) in zip(order, order[1:]))
print("FIFO:", fifo)
print("longest wait:", round(max(s - a for a, s in order)), "s")
```

This is not a bug in the loop, and no query will fix it. Plates are pushed in arrival order and
popped from the top, which is **non-preemptive LCFS** — last-come-first-served. Its mean wait is
identical to FIFO, because any work-conserving discipline that ignores service times leaves the same
work in the system. What changes is the tail: most plates go straight in, and one plate sits at the
bottom of the stacker while later arrivals are stacked on top of it and lifted back off.

Worth stating precisely, because it is the part that generalizes: **LIFO comes from the pair (push
order, pop end), not from the container.** Load the same stacker bottom-up in reverse and it serves
FIFO. The hardware constrains the discipline; it does not determine it.

### Exercise: what would a true FIFO stacker be?

The alternative PLR already models is random access — `pylabrobot.storage.Incubator`, with
independent sites and a loading tray, backed by Cytomat or Liconic hardware. Any plate is reachable,
so arrival order is yours to choose. It also costs more and takes more deck.

Between the two sits the bottom-feed destacker, which PLR does not model. Consider it from both
ends.

**Physically.** The bottom plate carries the weight of the stack, so dispensing it means holding
plate 2 while plate 1 leaves — fingers engaging a plate skirt, or a shaft that lifts the stack by one
pitch. What does that buy, and what does it cost in tooling that only fits one plate format? And what
is the alternative that needs no new mechanism at all — at the price of putting every plate through
two extra moves?

**As a PLR resource.** Subclass `ResourceStack`, add `get_bottom_item()`, and override the top-only
guard seen above. Then check the work against the resource tree:

```python
#| eval: false
print([(c.name, c.location.z) for c in stacker.children])
print(stacker.get_size_z())
```

Removing the bottom plate without re-settling the plates above it leaves a stack whose reported
height and whose children's positions disagree — the plates float. Chatterbox will not notice.
Custom resources are [chapter 17](../part4/17_custom_labware.qmd).

### Exercise: how old does the oldest plate get?

The run recorded `arrived` and `started` for every plate but never asked the question that matters.
Nothing here depends on the average wait; what matters is whether the oldest plate on the deck was
still good when it was processed.

```python
#| eval: false
db.execute("SELECT MAX(started - arrived) FROM plates").fetchone()[0]
```

That is one number from one run — a single draw. The simulation is seeded and costs no wall-clock
time, which is exactly what makes it cheap to ask for the distribution instead: re-run across seeds,
collect the maximum from each, and look at the spread. Two things to watch for:

- The mean wait will not move between LIFO and FIFO. The maximum will, by a lot. Whichever statistic
  is measured decides which conclusion is reached.
- The parameter governing both is the ratio of `SERVICE` to `MEAN_GAP`. Push it toward 1 and see
  which statistic degrades first.

If the tail is longer than the chemistry tolerates, the fix is not a better query. It is different
equipment.

:::

---

## What to remember

- Substitute time and measurements: a protocol that depends on a clock object and a seeded RNG can
  run instantly and reproduce a failing test.
- Seed the RNG (`random.Random(42)`) — stochastic, but deterministic.
- Keep the arithmetic that can be wrong in a plain function of numbers, separate from the robot, the
  database, and the clock.
- Test **invariants** — completion, ordering, tolerance to target, and physical position — rather
  than individual values. Set the tolerance wider than the simulated measurement noise.
- The resource tree is the check that a move was physically possible; chatterbox validates state,
  not physics.
- Queue discipline is a property of the equipment. A `ResourceStack` is a stack, and serving from it
  is LCFS: same mean wait as FIFO, much heavier tail.
